claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix has an FCC structure at 300 K.
The coating initially has a high dislocation density and nanosized precipitates.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has stable wear resistance and high elastic modulus at 300 K.
The alloy has high stacking-fault energy at room temperature.
Low room-temperature dislocation mobility maintains a stable dislocation network.
A stable dislocation network provides the high elastic modulus and wear resistance.
Increasing temperature produces lattice softening that lowers the Peierls barrier.
The reduced Peierls barrier promotes dislocation climb and cross-slip.
Low-temperature deformation is maintained by dislocation glide and climb controlled by lattice diffusion.
Dynamic recrystallization can occur under elevated temperature and stress in the 500–600 °C range.
Partial recrystallization becomes a deformation mechanism at about 700 °C or higher.
Above approximately 500–600 °C, thermal activation causes severe atomic disorder and accelerated diffusion.
Dynamic recrystallization is accompanied by intense solute diffusion, grain refinement, and increased opportunity for grain-boundary sliding.
Dynamic recrystallization and atomic disorder cause a sharp loss of wear resistance by reducing structural integrity and accelerating diffusion-controlled deformation.
The dominant mechanism changes from defect-mediated plasticity to rapid lattice disorder above approximately 500–600 °C.
Temperature-dependent evolution of dislocation density and stacking-fault energy leads to dynamic recrystallization and lattice disorder.
Conventional high-entropy alloys exhibit similar temperature-dependent wear behavior.
FeNiCrCoCu has enhanced room-temperature stability because of its specific composition.
The proposed mechanism applies to FCC high-entropy alloys with moderate stacking-fault energy.
Stable wear resistance above 600 °C in the absence of dynamic recrystallization would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The room-temperature explanation invokes high stacking-fault energy, whereas the stated applicability boundary specifies moderate stacking-fault energy; no evolution connecting these regimes is given.

The hypothesis presents climb as promoted as temperature rises, while the mechanism field already assigns lattice-diffusion-controlled climb to the low-temperature regime, leaving the claimed mechanistic shift poorly distinguished.
